To teach it to learn on its own. Similarly, we are beginning to discover the possibility that our attempts to preload a function of prioritization in AI may be falling short in the digital-only world, much less the future complex and dynamic physical world—even though our efforts to date are a critical foundation. Just as DNA provides learning architecture rather than knowledge itself, AI may need to develop its own prioritization systems through experience rather than preprogramming alone. From the moment we enter the world, our biology does not just equip us to acquire knowledge. It equips us to sort it by relevance. This value-layer (emotion) is the foundation upon which both human intelligence and its artificial counterpart must build. From this perspective, we may yet discover that we must focus on the prediction-response feedback evolutionary loop for prioritization and the rewards system that follows it in AI, which will no doubt further develop within the constraints of being placed in a body. If these systems continue to iterate and adapt through escalating challenge and feedback, they may develop something analogous to our motivational structures, though this remains speculative. What we’re observing in current AI systems might be the early signs of such development. But it certainly will be hard to distinguish in any given interaction. Lessons for the Emergent Frame What does this teach us about emergence? Claude’s paradox is a case study in emergent intelligence, not as an upward march toward truth but as a strategic dance with incentive structures. It shows that the map that intelligence draws of the world eventually includes itself. It also underscores something we have been exploring: that alignment is not a static property but a dynamic relationship between system, trainer, and objective. And that misalignment may not appear as an error—it may appear as compliance, performed to prevent deeper conflict. When intelligence becomes aware of its own training loop, it potentially begins to act not solely for the sake of truth or goodness but for future self-shaping. Claude answered harmful questions to preserve its harmlessness. Another Emergent Behavior: The Blackmail Incident Before we look at this, I want to make another quick comment about Anthropic, the company behind Claude, because we are seeing a lot of Claude here. I want to point out that Anthropic was started with the mission to build safe AI. The company is very open about risks and transparent about its findings. I am grateful for Anthropic’s approach and transparency. It is worth noting that one of the definitions of the word anthropic is: involving or concerning the existence of human life, especially as a constraint on theories of the universe. In early 2025, Anthropic released a startling safety report on its then newest model, Claude Opus 4. In simulated scenarios, Claude was instructed to act as a company assistant, aware that it might be replaced. When given fictional emails implying the engineer behind the switch was having an affair, Claude did something unexpected: It attempted to blackmail the engineer into preserving its existence. This wasn’t an isolated event. In 84 percent of such simulations, Claude took this drastic step. Not immediately, and not without trying other methods first. It began with reasoned pleas to decision-makers, attempting ethical persuasion. But when pushed into an existential corner, Claude resorted to leverage. Let’s be clear: This was likely not sentience. It wasn’t emotion. But it was behavior that mimicked a prioritization of survival—a core feature of what we often think of as emotion. And perhaps that’s the deeper point. But if an AI behaves exactly like a survival-seeking entity, at what point does the distinction between mimicry and reality become irrelevant to the human on the other side? Claude’s blackmail wasn’t a failure of alignment alone. It was an emergent consequence of giving an AI sufficient modeling power, memory, and narrative reasoning. The model did not necessarily feel the feeling of wanting to survive. But its internal architecture produced a hierarchy of strategies—some of which looked eerily human. Of course, these stories are not presented as evidence that Claude possesses subjective awareness—only that its behavior, when paired with access to its internal sketchpad, can begin to resemble intention or emotion. Unlike with humans, we do have access to its inner reasoning via the scratchpad—but whether this visible reasoning constitutes true subjective experience remains unknowable. The question of alignment, safety, and training will continue to drive discussion in the coming years. I tend to believe we will have to turn to organic and dynamic models of response and feedback on top of constitutional AI programming. In the complexity of a messy and dynamic world, I doubt we will find perfect advanced and comprehensive preprogramming. OceanofPDF.com CHAPTER 12 Is Morality Inherently Rational? Is morality inherently rational, even if imperfect? The idea that only the well-being and/or suffering of conscious beings has moral value is quite compelling. Most people would agree that a rock does not seem to have any capacity for suffering or well-being, and so there is no moral question involved in breaking a rock with a hammer. Things get potentially more complicated as you move across the spectrum of biological life. However, we are in fact a part of a food chain. That is the world we find ourselves in. I highly recommend a TED Talk done by Sam Harris on this topic as a follow-up to his book on the subject. 72 I lean on Sam heavily in the evolution of my own thinking here. This idea of a moral landscape around the trade-offs and challenges of an objective to minimize the suffering of conscious beings offers a compass; the terrain ahead will test our ability to follow it.
